children.html: The Role of Creative Potential and Intelligence for Humor Production
Raphaela Kellner and Mathias Benedek University of Graz

The ability to come up with good puns or jokes has been variantly viewed as an indicator of intelligence or creativity. Although the empirical literature provides support for both associations, it remains unclear whether intelligence and creativity independently contribute to the production of humor. To test this notion, a humor production test was devised that asked participants (n - 151) to generate funny punch lines to six captionremoved cartoons. The results showed that intelligence and creative potential predict humor production ability independently. Specifically, divergent thinking fluency and creativity as well as crystallized intelligence explained unique variance of the funniness of humor productions. These findings contribute to our understanding of the role of domain-general abilities involved in the production of humor.
Keywords: humor production, intelligence, creativity, divergent thinking

Almost everybody appreciates a good sense of humor. Humor has been viewed as a form of social play (Martin, 2003, 2009) and even as an instrument of social selection that signals relevant fitness-related traits (McGee & Shevlin, 2009; Storey, 2003). On the one hand, humor is viewed as an indicator of wit and hence intelligence (e.g., Greengross & Miller, 2011); on the other hand, humor has also been conceived as a domain-specific expression of creativity (e.g., Clabby, 1980). Both notions seem supported by the empirical literature to some extent. However, given that intelligence and creativity are related constructs that share cognitive mechanisms, it remains the question whether intelligence and creative potential independently contribute to humor.

Humor can be conceptualized in different ways. First, there is sense of humor, which is seen as an attitude or strategy for dealing with life's challenges (Humke & Schaefer, 1996; Thorson & Powell, 1993). Instead of being disconcerted a person with an adaptive sense of humor is able to laugh at the problem. Caricatures that are issued in newspapers and often depict elementary mistakes of politicians can be seen to support humorous coping strategies. A second conceptualization of humor refers to humor comprehension ability. It describes the ability to understand or "get" a humorous stimulus (Kozbelt & Nishioka, 2010). Importantly, the comprehension of humor will not necessarily imply that the person also evaluates it as being humorous. For instance, not all people like jokes at other people's expense, and sexual jokes are generally liked more by men than by women (Herzog, 1999), whereas women prefer nonsense humor compared to men (O'Connell, 1960). This third facet of humor is called

humor appreciation, reflecting preferences for certain humor styles that are also shaped by culture (Kaufman, Kozbelt, Bromley, & Miller, 2008). Finally, humor production ability refers to the ability to generate funny products (e.g., jokes, puns, stories, drawings) that are evaluated as humorous by other people (O'Quin & Derks, 2011). Producing humor seems most akin to creativity and hence it is the kind of humor trait we focus on in the present study.

There are different approaches to the assessment of humor production ability. Besides self-report questionnaires and external assessments also more objective performance measures are used. A common performance measure is the generation of punch lines (e.g., Brodzinsky & Rubien, 1976; Greengross, Martin, & Miller, 2012; Greengross & Miller, 2011; Koppel & Sechrest, 1970; Treadwell, 1970). People are shown photos or caption-removed cartoons and asked to produce funny punch lines within a given frame. The captions are subsequently evaluated for humor by independent judges. One example is the Cartoon Production Punchline Test (CPPT; Köhler & Ruch, 1993), which includes cartoons considering three different humor appreciation categories: incongruity-resolution, nonsense, and sexual humor. In the category incongruity-resolution, a paradox situation is to be resolved by the punch line. In the nonsense category, the encountered paradox cannot be completely solved and the punch line may even lead to further discrepancies. The sexual category refers explicitly to sexual contents. Caption-removed cartoons are among of the most frequently used humor productions tests, but also other tests exist that ask for the generation of funny texts for portraits or hypothetic situations or to draw funny pictures of a given object or creature (e.g., Howrigan & MacDonald, 2008).

Humor has been viewed as an indicator of intelligence (Greengross & Miller, 2011; Kaufman et al., 2008). Several studies have asserted that intelligence is related to humor comprehension and humor knowledge (e.g., Couturier, Mansfield, & Gallagher, 1981; Feingold, 1983). also associated with humor production. Koppel and Sechrest (1970) used a test with 20 caption-removed cartoons and found a modest correlation between intelligence and the rated funniness of responses (r = .23). Howrigan and MacDonald (2008) used various verbal tasks (i.e., completing character profiles, answering questions about hypothetic situations) and nonverbal tasks (e.g., drawing of animals) and observed a moderate correlation of a compound humor production measure with intelligence (r = .29). Greengross and Miller (2011) observed similar relationships between humor production ability (three cartoons) and fluid intelligence (r = .24) or verbal intelligence (r = .31). In another study by Greengross et al. (2012), humor production ability, intelligence, and several personality traits were compared between professional stand-up comedians and university students. They found that stand-up comedians generated funnier cartoon captions and also showed higher verbal intelligence. Moreover, humor production ability was significantly correlated with verbal intelligence in the students (r = .39) but not in the relatively small sample of 31 comedians. These findings consistently support that intelligence predicts humor production ability.

Humor also shows obvious conceptual similarities with creativity: Both require finding solutions that link disparities in an original way and thereby elicit surprise (O'Quin & Derks, 2011; Rouff, 1975). Clabby (1980) proposed that humorous people "are creative in that they condense seemingly unrelated thoughts in odd ways to fulfill the useful purpose of entertainment" (p. 309). Humor production hence could be seen as an expression of (domain-general) creative potential applied to the domain of humor.

A few studies empirically examined the relationship between creative potential and humor production ability. For example, Brodzinsky and Rubien (1976) found that people scoring high versus low in the Remote Associates Test (RAT; Mednick, 1962) showed higher humor production ability as measured by a captionremoved cartoon test. Similarly, Treadwell (1970) reported that humor production ability in the cartoon test was related to higher creativity as evidenced in higher performance in the RAT, in a Gestalt production test, and in a novelty production scoring of the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT; Maddi & Berne, 1964) with correlations ranging between .24 and .28. In a study by Fabrizi and Pollio (1987), school students were observed and scored for how often they made their peers laugh. They found positive correlations between individual laughing rates and creative potential measured with the figural version of the Torrance Test of Creative Thinking (TTCT) as well as with teacher ratings of creativity in 11th graders but not in 7th graders. Another study asked participants to write five funny texts which were evaluated for humor and collected creativity and verbal fluency measures (Clabby, 1980). They found that humor production ability was moderately correlated with creativity assessed with the alternate uses task (r = .33) but not with verbal fluency. These findings suggest a positive correlation between humor production and creativity; it should be noted, however, that a couple of other studies found no robust correlation between humor production tests and creativity measures (Babad, 1974; Schoel & Busse, 1971).

Intelligence and creativity (in terms of creative potential) are domain-general cognitive abilities that underlie many more complex, domain-specific abilities and skills. The available literature provides evidence that humor production ability is related to both intelligence and creativity. So far, however, no study seems to have tested whether intelligence and creativity contribute independently to humor production ability. Considering that intelligence and creativity are correlated themselves (e.g., Jauk et al., 2013; Kim, 2005; Silvia, 2008) and assumed to share basic cognitive mechanisms (e.g., Benedek et al., 2014b; Nusbaum & Silvia, 2011), it remains the question whether creativity and intelligence still predict humor production once the other predictor is taken into account.

Another reason for this study is that much of the evidence of humor production and creativity is based on the RAT, a task that is often viewed to reflect convergent thinking or at most convergent creativity (Lee, Huggins, & Therriault, 2014; Smith, Huber, & Vul, 2013). In contrast, relatively little is known about the role of divergent thinking ability for humor production, a common indicator of creative potential that has seen much development with respect to scoring methods over the last years. Specifically, the top-scoring method was proposed to yield a valid indicator of ideational creativity that is less dependent on ideational fluency than other scores like for example, uniqueness scoring (Benedek et al., 2013; Silvia et al., 2008).

The present study hence assessed humor production ability, intelligence, and creativity and tested whether domain-general indicators of cognitive ability (i.e., intelligence and creativity) independently predict the potentially more complex trait of humor production ability. Finally, to better understand the role of intelligence for humor production, we considered fluid and crystallized intelligence as two distinguishable facets of intelligence (Horn & Cattell, 1966). Greengross and Miller (2011) found that verbal intelligence was a better predictor for humor production than fluid intelligence. Because verbal intelligence is commonly assessed with tests requiring vocabulary knowledge, we expected that crystallized intelligence may be more relevant than fluid intelligence for humor production.

One hundred fifty-two people participated in the present study. One person had to be excluded, because he had failed to generate any responses in the humor test. Unless noted otherwise, the final sample hence included 151 participants (72.8% females; M=23.1,\ SD=5.2). The sample was recruited via email lists and announcements on the university campus. It hence reflected a student sample (96.7% students) with a large proportion majoring in psychology (69.5%). The participants either participated in partial fulfilment of course credit or received a bar of chocolate. All participants gave their written informed consent.
Humor production ability. We devised a humor production test (HPT) based on Köhler's and Ruch's (1993) CPPT to assess

humor production ability. This test presents caption-removed cartoons and asks to generate humorous punch lines. As in the CPPT, the tasks were designed to reflect three different humor appreciation categories, including incongruity-resolution humor (INC), nonsense humor (NON), and sexual humor (SEX). The cartoons were newly devised to compile a set of colored, high-resolution (1,500 \times 1,500 \text{ pixel}) digital image tasks that can be used for future research. Initially, nine colored cartoons were drawn by the first author (three of each humor category), with two of them representing conceptual adaptations from the CPPT. All of them illustrate social interactions that should facilitate the creation of humorous punch lines (Martin, 2003). Furthermore, it was ensured that the images alone were not too funny or obvious, permitting that participants find their own interpretation of the incongruities and generate their individual humorous solutions. We conducted a small pilot study and excluded one task per category that showed the lowest number of responses. The final HPT hence included six items (i.e., INC: tasks cow and skeleton; NON: tasks apple and animals; SEX: tasks bed and exhibitionist). The test materials of the HPT are available from the authors on request.

Participants received a written instruction for the test. They were told that many cartoons only become funny due to its punch line, which was demonstrated by an example. Subsequently, a second example of a caption-removed cartoon served as a practice task. Participants were instructed to write down all humorous punch lines that they could think of. After the instruction, the HPT tasks were presented with the aid of Matlab scripts for 2.5 min per cartoon in an individually randomized sequence. Punch line responses were written on a response sheet. Each task was followed by a 10-s pause to allow finishing already begun responses. After the test, the participants were asked to rank their punch lines from the most funny to the least funny per cartoon. The total duration of the HPT was about 25 min.

Participants generated on average two to three punch lines per humor task (M=2.59,\ SD=1.16). Virtually all participants generated at least one response on average (99%), but only 60% of the sample came up with two or more responses.

The HPT responses were evaluated for funniness by 10 independent judges. Responses were digitalized and alphabetically sorted across all participants per cartoon. This procedure ensured that factors like handwriting or number of solutions per individual cannot influence the ratings. The judges were made familiar with the test by skimming over all responses of a task before rating the punch lines. Each response was evaluated on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not funny) to 3 (very funny). In the rare case that no response was given (0-2% per task) that task was scored as 0. The interrater reliability in the six tasks ranged from ICC(3,k) =.67 to .81 (on average: .75) suggesting good interrater agreement in the evaluation of the funniness of individual punch lines. For each participant we selected the funniest caption per task (according to averaged ratings), which can be seen as most representative of the participant's humor production ability (Greengross & Miller, 2011; Köhler & Ruch, 1996). The ratings of the funniest captions per task were then averaged across tasks to obtain a total index of individual humor production ability. While the interrater reliability across the 10 judges (considering the ratings of the selected funniest responses averaged across the six tasks) was high ICC(3,k) = .88, the internal consistency across the six tasks (considering the ratings of the selected funniest responses aver-

aged across the 10 raters) was low (Cronbach's alpha = .52). The judges hence showed good agreement in their evaluations, but the performance in individual tasks was only modestly related. The low internal consistency may in part be due to the three different humor categories implemented in the HPT. In cases of heterogeneous constructs, internal consistency typically underestimates actual reliability (McCrae et al., 2011).

Self-report of humor production ability. To measure self-reported humor production ability, we created a short scale by selecting five items from the Multidimensional Sense of Humor Scale (Thorson & Powell, 1993) with high factor loadings on the humor generation or creativity factor (e.g., "I can say things in such a way as to make people laugh"). Participants responded on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (I strongly disagree) to 4 (I strongly agree). One person failed to respond on this task resulting in a missing value for this measure. The internal consistency of this self-report humor measure was good (Cronbach's alpha = .76).

Divergent thinking. Divergent thinking (DT) ability or creative potential was assessed with four divergent thinking tasks, two alternate uses tasks and two instances tasks. The alternate uses tasks asked to generate creative uses for a car tire and a knife. The instances tasks asked to generate creative solutions to the problems "What makes noise?" and "What can be used for quicker locomotion?". In all DT tasks, participants were asked to generate responses that should be as creative as possible. Tasks were presented via Matlab scripts and responses were entered in the program. The task duration was 2.5 min. After the tasks were completed participants were once more shown their responses and asked to select the three most creative responses per task. The data of one person was lost due to technical issues resulting in one missing value for this measure.

Task performance was scored for fluency and creativity. DT fluency reflected the number of ideas per task. For the scoring of DT creativity, we computed a top-3 creativity score (Benedek et al., 2013). The self-selected three most creative ideas were evaluated by five judges on a 4-point Likert format ranging from 0 (not creative) to 3 (very creative). The rating procedure was similar as for the humor responses, and the interrater reliability ranged from .59 to .71. The creativity evaluations were then averaged across judges and the three ideas per task. The internal consistency across the four tasks was satisfactory (Cronbach's alpha = .65).

Intelligence. Intelligence was assessed with four tasks, two measures of fluid intelligence and two measures of crystallized intelligence (Horn & Cattell, 1966). Fluid intelligence measures included the series completion task and the matrices task of the Culture Fair Test 3 (Cattell & Weiß, 1971). The tasks required to identify rules behind series or matrices of symbols. The tasks included 13 items each and were timed 3 min. Crystallized intelligence measures included the synonyms and the sayings tasks from the Wilde-Intelligence-Test (Jäger & Althoff, 1983). In the synonyms task, participants had to identify the most adequate synonyms among five options (2 min to solve 20 items). Similarly, in the sayings task participants were presented one saying and had to identify another saying with the same meaning among five options (4.5 min to solve 16 items). We computed scores of fluid intelligence (Gf) and crystallized intelligence (Gc) by averaging across the z-standardized scores of the series and matrices task, and the synonyms and sayings tasks, respectively. A total intelligence score was also computed as the average of the Gf and Gc score.

Creative achievement. We assessed creative achievements with the top-5 creative achievement scale of the German version of the Inventory of Creative Activities and Achievements (ICAA; Benedek & Jauk, 2012). This scale asks to list the five most creative achievements of one's life. There was no time restriction for the participants. Five raters scored the answers on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not creative) to 4 (highly creative). If less than five achievements were reported 0 points were awarded for missing achievements. The interrater reliability was .73, and the internal consistency across the five achievements was Cronbach's alpha = .67. A total creative achievements. This measure was included following conventions of our lab, but we had no hypotheses regarding this measure and hence only report general correlational findings.

The subjects were tested in groups of up to seven people. The participants read an information sheet and signed their informed consent. A sociodemographic questionnaire assessed relevant information about the participants (e.g., age, gender, highest education). The test session began with the self-report of humor production ability followed by the HPT. Afterward, intelligence and divergent thinking ability were assessed in balanced order to control potential position effects. Also the order of fluid and crystallized intelligence tasks was balanced. Finally, participants completed the creative achievements questionnaire. The total duration of the test session was about 90 min. The experiment was approved by the local ethics committee.

Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics for the six humor production tasks. Average funniness evaluations were close to 1 suggesting rather low rated funniness in general. Correlations between tasks were all positive and ranged from nonsignificant coefficients up to .29. Because correlations between tasks of the same humor appreciation category (i.e., INC, NON, and SEX) were not necessarily higher than between categories, it did not seem appropriate to compute separate category-specific humor production scores. The correlations of humor production with creativity and intelligence measures are presented in Table 2. Humor production ability as measured with the HPT was significantly correlated with measures of creative potential (i.e., DT fluency and creativity) as well as with intelligence. In contrast, self-reported humor production ability showed only a modest correlation with DT fluency, but with none of the other measures. Critically, self-reported humor was not significantly correlated with actual humor production measured by a performance test.

The findings suggest that creativity and intelligence measures are correlated to humor production at roughly the same level. In a next step, we tested whether creativity and intelligence actually explain unique variance in humor production ability or whether part of these correlations is due to overlapping variance of the predictors. To this end, we computed a regression analysis where humor production ability was predicted by DT fluency and creativity and by the aggregated intelligence measure. This analysis revealed that all three measures independently predict humor production ability, R_{adj}^2 = .15; F(3, 146) = 9.43, p < .001 (see Table 3, Model 1).

We finally examined to what extent the significant prediction of humor production by intelligence can be attributed to the intelligence facets of Gf and Gc. We hence computed another regression analysis replacing the aggregated intelligence measure with Gf and Gc scores. This analysis showed that humor production ability is significantly predicted by Gc but not by Gf, R_{adj}^2 = .16; F(3, 145) = 8.28, p < .001 (see Table 3, Model 2).
Does Humor Production Rely on Intelligence and Creativity?

The main aim of this study was to investigate whether humor production ability relies on intelligence, creativity, or both. First of all, our study replicated previous findings showing that humor production is correlated with intelligence (Greengross & Miller, 2011; Greengross et al., 2012; Howrigan & MacDonald, 2008; Koppel & Sechrest, 1970), as well as with creativity (Brodzinsky & Rubien, 1976; Clabby, 1980; Fabrizi & Pollio, 1987; Treadwell, 1970). In other words, people scoring higher on intelligence tests and on divergent thinking (DT) tests also produced funnier punch lines in the humor production test. The findings further extended previous research in showing that intelligence and creativity predict humor production ability independently. This is not selfevident, because creativity and intelligence are typically found to be correlated themselves (e.g., Jauk et al., 2013; Kim, 2005; Nusbaum et al., 2011; Silvia, 2015), and hence relationships of one construct with humor production might be attenuated when controlling for the other. Regression analyses, however, showed that creativity and intelligence actually both explain unique variance in the ability of being funny.

This study is also the first to show that the creativity-humor association generalizes to creativity measured by rated DT performance. Previous humor studies often measured creativity with the RAT (Mednick, 1962). But the RAT is sometimes seen as a convergent thinking task (Lee et al., 2014), and it has an obvious verbal component that may as well be relevant in humor production. Other humor studies used DT tasks, but they either used a uniqueness scoring (Clabby, 1980), or the standard TTCT scoring. These traditional scorings are efficient but the resulting creativity measures are known to be highly dependent on ideational fluency (Hocevar, 1979; Michael & Wright, 1989). In our study, we thus assessed DT creativity with the subjective top-scoring method (Benedek et al., 2013; Silvia et al., 2008) that avoids direct dependency on ideational fluency.

We found that DT fluency and DT creativity independently predicted humor production ability. DT fluency and DT creativity represent two aspects of creative potential: DT fluency captures how easily we can generate novel ideas; DT creativity reflects how effectively we can come up with something novel that also strikes others as being interesting or clever (Wilson, Guilford, & Christensen, 1953) by integrating remotely associated constructs in an appropriate way (Mednick, 1962). These capacities appear clearly relevant to humor production that has been defined as the generation of something novel that resolves disparities in a surprising and clever way (O'Quin & Derks, 2011; Rouff, 1975). Humor production hence could be seen as an expression of (domaingeneral) creative potential applied to the domain of humor. This

finding complements previous research showing that DT ability is relevant in the domains of dance or music (Benedek et al., 2014a; Fink & Woschnjak, 2011). One might potentially even go one step further and conceive humor production as a domain-specific expression of divergent thinking. It should be noted, however, that ideas can be creative in many other ways than by being funny (e.g., Silvia et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 1953), and that humor is usually conceived as just one of many different domains of creativity (cf. Carson, Peterson, & Higgins, 2005).

The fact that DT fluency and creativity independently predicted the funniness of humor productions seems also noteworthy from a psychometric perspective. As previously noted, it has been questioned whether fluency and originality actually show discriminant validity (Hocevar, 1979; Michael & Wright, 1989). Our results suggest that DT fluency and creativity, when scored in a way that avoids a necessary confound, can be largely independent, yet complementally valid indicators of creative potential. This finding is consistent with a previous study showing that DT fluency and creativity are independent predictors of the frequency to engage in creative activities (Jauk, Benedek, & Neubauer, 2014).

As expected, humor production was found to be more strongly predicted by Gc than by Gf (which was no significant predictor in this study). This is consistent with the findings by Greengross and Miller (2011), who reported that humor production ability showed higher correlations with performance in a vocabulary test than with performance in the Raven's task, which are common indicators of crystallized and fluid intelligence (Horn & Cattell, 1966). This finding further specifies the intelligence-humor relationship. It emphasizes to the knowledge-dependent and verbal nature of humor production. Many puns appear to essentially reflect a clever play on words. As a consequence, eloquence and high proficiency in the subtleties of language may represent a central prerequisite for being funny, just as the best joke can be spoiled when not told the right way. The higher relevance of acquired knowledge over fluid intelligence for humor production ability, together with the absence of gender differences in humor ability, also challenges evolutionary interpretations of the humor-intelligence relationship (cf. Greengross & Miller, 2011; Mickes et al., 2012).

The consideration of intelligence factors has also been fruitfully applied to the understanding of creative metaphor production (Beaty & Silvia, 2013). Interestingly, creativity metaphor production was found to be more dependent on fluid intelligence and broad retrieval ability than on crystallized intelligence. Although
metaphor production can also be viewed as a verbal task, the discrepant findings suggest that metaphor production and humor production rely on different pattern of cognitive abilities.

We were concerned about the low internal consistency of the employed humor production test. Although the assessment of humor production ability commonly relies on the caption-removed cartoon task, its internal consistency is often found to be modest (e.g., Köhler & Ruch, 1996; Masten, 1986). Yet, low internal consistency does not necessarily imply low reliability, because internal consistency measures underestimate the reliability of heterogeneous or multidimensional measures (McCrae et al., 2011). The employed humor production test was designed to capture humor ability in three different humor styles in order to acknowledge individual differences in humor appreciation (Kaufman et al., 2008; Köhler & Ruch, 1993). While the test attempted to provide broad opportunity to show one's humor production ability, we assume that humor production will generally work better for tasks that are conducive to one's preferred humor style. Moreover, humor appreciation may also play an important role at the level of judges who scored the punch lines, although good interrater reliability suggests that judges generally showed reasonable agreement in the evaluation of individual responses. A broadly conceptualized humor test hence may imply low internal consistency, but still show good reliability or validity, which seems supported by substantial correlations between humor production ability and measures of creativity and intelligence. Future research may assess reliability beyond internal consistency (e.g., retest reliability) and examine potential person-task and rater-task interactions depending on individual humor appreciation styles. Another critical point refers to the external validity of the test. Humor is usually displayed in relaxed social interactions (Babad, 1974), which cannot be easily established in test labs.

It should further be acknowledged that the conceptual overlap between humor production and divergent thinking also implied a methodological overlap in their assessment. DT tasks and the humor production test asked people to generate original solutions to open problems in a timed task. The correlation between these constructs hence may have been increased by shared method variance. It should be noted, however, that a different study, which measured humor by scoring how often people made others laugh in social situations, still observed a significant correlation of their humor index with divergent thinking ability (Fabrizi & Pollio, 1987).

Finally, we noticed that fluid intelligence and DT ability were uncorrelated in this study, which is an unexpected finding, given the robust positive correlations in previous research. We used well-established, brief intelligence tests as they are commonly used in this kind of research. Closer examinations of the scores did not reveal evidence for restricted variability such as ceiling effects.

Our study replicated the findings that humor production is correlated to intelligence and creativity. We extended previous findings by showing that humor production ability is independently predicted by measures of creativity and intelligence. Spe-

cifically, the funniness of humorous ideas relies on DT fluency, DT creativity, and crystallized intelligence. These findings highlight the relevance of a set of different domain-general cognitive abilities for being funny.
